extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and critics of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the methods by which a novelist should select, arrange and present material: how to choose and fix a subject, manage point of view, balance scene and summary, and keep method consistent to achieve the desired artistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be 'absolutely true to themselves' — wherever we meet them they remain the people we know, changing only under the touch of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent traits and behavior for characters so that their actions are believable throughout the work; character truthfulness is distinct from the story's shape. Example/contrast: Tolstoy's characters remain consistent even when the story's focus wanders. Anti-pattern: creating characters who act out of character merely to serve plot convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial purpose / fixed subject
rubrics_metrics.description: 'His subject... was rooted in his thought, and never left its place by a hair's breadth' — the novelist should have a clear, fixed subject or design for the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide and keep hold of the book's central subject or intention while writing. Flaubert is praised for keeping his subject quiescent; danger arises when the author vacillates or allows the subject to drift, wasting material and weakening the overall effect. If the subject changes unintentionally, the book's representative character can be lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use facts to express meaning (show, don't merely state)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is 'not a row of facts, it is a single image; the facts are nothing until they have been used' — a novelist should present facts so they announce the meaning he sees in them rather than merely reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and arrange facts to create an effect or image; avoid mere information-dumping or external attestation. Narrative must 'look true' on its own terms. Anti-pattern: treating a novel like an official report or relying on external proof instead of making the book feel true by its own method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful selection of information / method of presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's method is the manner of choosing his path — how he selects the information he offers and places his statements; the whole interest lies in that selection and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate about what is shown, what is summarized, and what background the author supplies. Vary methods (direct description, authorial recall, interior access) purposefully, and be aware that these shifts are fundamental choices about the reader's relation to the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish and manage scenic vs panoramic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a necessary alternative between a 'scenic' presentation (a particular scene/hour) and a 'panoramic' presentation (surveying lives from a height).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose when to place the reader in an immediate scene and when to step back for summary or sweep. Watch how alternation is managed; scenes often open interest and lead to climaxes, while panoramas give breadth. Anti-pattern: jarring, unprepared jumps between scene and panorama that confuse the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / centre of vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide 'with which of the characters, if with any of them, is the writer to identify himself' — which mind to 'go behind' and how often to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a primary centre of consciousness and avoid unnecessary, haphazard plunges into other characters' inner lives. If the subject can be rendered from one character's perspective, prefer that consistency. Example: Madame Bovary is primarily seen through Emma's eyes; occasional shifts must be justified by the subject's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial voice vs dramatization through characters (impersonality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'impersonality' of a writer means not announcing opinions outright but dramatizing them in living form; whether the author speaks in his own voice or through a character is a deliberate method choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide how overt the author's presence should be. Even when subtle, the author's judgement is embodied in the presentation. Use tact to dramatize opinions rather than state them directly when desired; when authorial intervention is needed, supply it carefully to illuminate rather than dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (subjective/mood) vs dramatic (objective/incidents) treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Material may be treated pictorially (as it appears in someone's mood or imagination) or dramatically (objective presentation of incidents/dialogue); the choice affects the reader's experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pictorial treatment to convey mood and subjective colour (e.g., filtered through a character's sensibility); use dramatic treatment when events should stand on their own and be witnessed. Flaubert mixes both depending on effect; choose whichever best serves the subject at each moment. Anti-pattern: treating a scene pictorially when the effect depends on objective detail (or vice versa), losing intended impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place scenes only when fully prepared (scene placement and preparation)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The placing of this occasion, at the point where everything is ready for it... is among the chief cares of the author' — scenes must be placed where action is ripe and resonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each scene has been prepared by prior summary or incidents so it can fulfill its dramatic purpose. Avoid scenes that do nothing or are unprepared, since they weaken a story. Scenes are often the means of starting interest and completing it at climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of latitude / follow a principle consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: The only law that binds the novelist is 'the need to be consistent on some plan' and to 'allow himself no more latitude than he requires.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a governing principle or plan for the book's methods and stick to it as far as necessary. Don't change methods gratuitously; reserve deviations for clear, compensating gains. This discipline keeps the work coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage alternation and layering of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods can be 'laid upon method' to create layers and stratifications in treatment — dramatic action treated pictorially, pictorial description rendered dramatically, points of view blended, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine techniques to suit the theme: alternate, unite, or superimpose methods when it serves the subject. A critic should look for the principle on which these mixtures rest. Be mindful that such fusion should reveal the subject, not obscure it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch how much authorial intervention the reader needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes 'it is necessary for us to know more than we could have made out by simply looking and listening' — the author must decide when to intervene with superior knowledge (backstory, inner thought) to illuminate the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authorial intrusion to supply necessary context, explain motivations, or reveal inner states that the scene alone cannot. But intervene only where it aids understanding; unnecessary authorial exposition can diminish the story's shown immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wasting material by lack of plan
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author 'ranged around his mountain of material, attacking it now here and now there, never deciding in his mind to what end he had amassed it', then great masses of life are wasted and weaken the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize and economize material so each item contributes to the book's design. Resist including charming but irrelevant episodes that do not advance the subject or enrich the central image; otherwise, the surplus material can dilute the overall effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure scenes form the book's articulation (structure by scenes and summaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: In well-crafted novels scenes (e.g., ball, market, theatre, interview, deathbed) form the articulation and scheme of structure; summaries carry the action on between scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the novel's structure so that key scenes articulate stages of the story and summaries link them purposefully. Each scene should 'take up the story, conclusively establish one aspect of it and open the view towards the next.' Use summaries economically to advance time or prepare the next scene.
